Fit a higher order Markov chain

Source: R/fitHigherOrder.R
fitHigherOrder.Rd

Fits the higher order Markov chain of Ching et al., in which the distribution of the next state is a weighted mixture of the empirical lag-\(i\) transition matrices, \(i = 1, \dots,\) order. seq2freqProb() returns the state frequencies of a sequence and seq2matHigh() its empirical lag-order transition matrix, the building blocks of the model.

Usage

fitHigherOrder(sequence, order = 2, method = c("mle", "lsq"))
seq2freqProb(sequence)
seq2matHigh(sequence, order)

Arguments

sequence

The sequence of states: a character vector, or a vector coercible to character (numbers and factors are matched to the states as character strings), without missing values. A list of such vectors is taken as independent sequences, see Details.

order

Order of the chain, a positive integer smaller than the sequence length; for seq2matHigh(), the lag.

method

How the weights \(\lambda\) are estimated: "mle" (default) or "lsq", see Details.

Value

fitHigherOrder(): a list with lambda, the weights of the lags; Q, the list of the lag-\(i\) transition matrices (column-stochastic: entry \([j, k]\) is the probability of moving to \(j\) from \(k\)); and X, the state frequencies. With method = "lsq", NULL with a warning if Rsolnp is not available.

seq2freqProb(): the vector of state frequencies, named by state. seq2matHigh(): the column-stochastic lag-order transition matrix (a state never observed as a departure state gets a uniform column).

Details

The fitted model expresses the distribution of the next state as the mixture \(\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i Q_i x_{t-i}\) of the empirical lag-\(i\) transition matrices \(Q_i\) (see seq2matHigh), with weights \(\lambda_i \ge 0\) summing to one. The matrices \(Q_i\) are the same for both methods; only the weights differ.

method = "lsq" (the default before version 1.2.1, and the only method before the argument existed) chooses \(\lambda\) to minimize the squared distance between the stationary distribution and its image under the mixture, as in Ching et al.; it needs the Rsolnp package and returns NULL with a warning if it is unavailable. This criterion is weak: each lag matrix maps the empirical distribution onto itself up to end effects, \(Q_i X \approx X\) with an error of order \(i/n\), so the objective is nearly flat in \(\lambda\) and the weights it returns can be unstable from one sample to another. It remains available, to reproduce earlier results or the method of Ching et al., but it is no longer the default.

method = "mle" (the default) chooses \(\lambda\) to maximize the log-likelihood \(\sum_{t=k+1}^{n} \log \sum_i \lambda_i Q_i[x_t, x_{t-i}]\) of the observations a model of order \(k\) can predict. For fixed \(Q_i\) the problem is concave, so the maximum is global, and it is solved, without Rsolnp, by Newton's method with an active set on the simplex, which stops when the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions of the maximum hold within \(10^{-10}\) (in practice after 3 to 10 iterations, also when some weights are 0). The weights are therefore those that give the highest value of higherOrderLogLik for the same observations. (Up to version 1.2 the EM algorithm for mixture weights was used: near a weight equal to 0, or when the lags carry nearly the same information, it converged very slowly and could stop visibly short of the maximum.) They are maximum likelihood estimates conditional on the empirical matrices \(Q_i\), which are not re-estimated: this is not the maximum likelihood estimator of the mixture with free matrices, in which the weights are in general not identifiable (a common distribution can be moved from \(\lambda_j Q_j\) to \(\lambda_i Q_i\) without changing any transition probability), so the weights should not be read as the relative importance of the lags beyond this conditional sense. Note that this is not the mixture transition distribution model of Raftery (1985), in which a single matrix is shared by all lags and is estimated together with the weights; that model is fitted by fitMTD.

With a list of sequences the lag matrices \(Q_i\) and the state frequencies are computed from the counts pooled over the sequences, which are treated as independent: no pair of observations spans two sequences, and a sequence with no more than order states contributes to the frequencies only. The weights are then estimated as for a single sequence, from the observations that a model of that order can predict in every sequence.

A warning is given when the sequence supplies no more observations than the model has free parameters (the number used by higherOrderLogLik), since the weights are then essentially undetermined.

References

Ching, W. K., Huang, X., Ng, M. K., & Siu, T. K. (2013). Higher-order markov chains. In Markov Chains (pp. 141-176). Springer US.

Ching, W.-K., Ng, M. K. and Fung, E. S. (2008). Higher-order multivariate Markov chains and their applications. Linear Algebra and its Applications 428(2-3), 492-507. doi:10.1016/j.laa.2007.05.021

Raftery, A. E. (1985). A model for high-order Markov chains. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 47(3), 528-539.

See also

higherOrderLogLik(), higherOrderPredict(), fitMTD(), selectOrder()

Other higher order chains: fitHighOrderMultivarMC(), predictHommc()

Author

Giorgio Spedicato, Tae Seung Kang

Examples

sequence<-c("a", "a", "b", "b", "a", "c", "b", "a", "b", "c", "a", "b",
            "c", "a", "b", "c", "a", "b", "a", "b")
# weights by maximum likelihood (the default, no Rsolnp needed)
fit <- fitHigherOrder(sequence, order = 2)
fit$lambda
#> [1] 1 0
# weights by least squares on the stationary distribution, as in Ching et al.
fitHigherOrder(sequence, order = 2, method = "lsq")
#> $lambda
#> [1] 1.000000e+00 1.852742e-09
#> 
#> $Q
#> $Q[[1]]
#>       a         b    c
#> a 0.125 0.4285714 0.75
#> b 0.750 0.1428571 0.25
#> c 0.125 0.4285714 0.00
#> 
#> $Q[[2]]
#>           a         b    c
#> a 0.1428571 0.5714286 0.25
#> b 0.4285714 0.2857143 0.75
#> c 0.4285714 0.1428571 0.00
#> 
#> 
#> $X
#>   a   b   c 
#> 0.4 0.4 0.2 
#> 
higherOrderLogLik(sequence, fit)$logLik
#> [1] -13.08457
